title: MB0-00957
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is the decision for XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, (claimant), a 25 year old Tamil male, citizen of Sri Lanka, who is seeking refugee protection in Canada pursuant to section 96 and section 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1.
The claimant alleged a risk of future persecution based on his race, religion, nationality and membership in a particular social group if he were to return to Sri Lanka.
The claimant alleged that he faced persecution dating back to mid 2001, at the hands of the Sri Lankan army.
The claimant alleged a fear of the Eelam People's Democratic Party (EPDP) since XXX 2006, because they abducted the claimant's father and only released the claimant's father upon payment of a bribe.
The claimant stated that his older brother was arrested by the military in XXXX of 2006, that he left Sri Lanka in XXX of 2007 and filed for refugee protection in Canada and was accepted.

The claimant alleged that he was arrested and detained by the military in XXXX of 2007 for one day and then again in XXXXXX 2007 when he was allegedly assaulted with a gun butt yet released after one hour.

The claimant left Sri Lanka in XXXX of 2008. The claimant alleged that he was then detained in the U.S. for approximately one year and seven months from XXXX 2008 until XXXX 2010. Upon release from detention in the U.S. the claimant came to Canada on XXXX, 2010 and filed a claim for refugee protection.

The Tribunal finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of IRPA, because notwithstanding a nexus to a Convention ground given his Tamil ethnicity, the Tribunal did not believe that the claimant credibly established that he was ever seriously considered a person of interest to the Sri Lankan army. Nor did the claimant credibly establish that he was being persecuted by anyone, nor that he would face a serious possibility of a risk of persecution were he to return to Sri Lanka in 2011. Further, the Tribunal found that even if the claimant's narrative were to be found credible, the claimant would not have been a Convention refugee due to the fact that there has been a change of circumstances in Sri Lanka. Notwithstanding that the situation may not be completely resolved, the Tribunal finds that from the available information, there would no longer be an objective basis for his fear.

The Tribunal also finds that the claimant is not a person in need of protection, based on a balance of probabilities, for a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, pursuant to section 97(1)(b) of IRPA. Nor that he would be subject to a danger of torture, pursuant to section 97(1)(a) of IRPA should he return to Sri Lanka.

The determinative issues are credibility, whether there is a personal risk of harm to the claimant today, whether there is a viable internal flight alternative and change of circumstances. ANALYSIS Identity

The Tribunal accepts the photocopies of the claimant's Sri Lankan passport, birth certificate and all related documentation seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada. The Tribunal accepts that the claimant is a citizen of Sri Lanka2. Credibility

At the beginning of the hearing the claimant testified that his personal information form (PIF) was true, accurate and up to date. The Tribunal found that his testimony was lacking in credibility that he was being personally targeted or seriously pursued in any manner. When questioned, the claimant could provide limited information, experienced limited incidents and failed to provide any documentation to corroborate his story. Further, notwithstanding that he claimed that his story was true, accurate, correct and up to date during his oral testimony he added an additional alleged detention that occurred in the XXXX month (XXXXXX) of 2007. The claimant had to be asked why he omitted this information multiple times. He initially told the Tribunal that he did not understand the question. Upon rephrasing of the question by the Board member, the tribunal officer and then again by his counsel, the claimant finally testified that he forgot. The Tribunal noted that the claimant included information and dates regarding his father's alleged abduction by the EPDP, his brother's alleged detention by the army in XXXX 2006, his friend's two week detention in XXXXXX 2007, but forgot to mention in either his POE application form, POE interview or PIF narrative, that the claimant himself encountered a separate detention in XXXXXX of 2007. The Tribunal found the omission negatively impacted on the claimant's credibility.

The Tribunal found that the claimant failed to explain why, during his alleged detentions (one in 2001 with other students where he was made to stand in the hot sun for an hour or two, one in XXXX of 2007 when he was allegedly held for a day after a bomb explosion that occurred directly in front of his house and once for an hour in XXXXXX of 2007), if he was a person of interest he would be detained so briefly in 2001, experience no issues for six years until 2007 when he was also allegedly detained briefly and released on both occasions in less than a day with some noted injuries (broken teeth), but nothing for which medical attention was required or a medical report could be produced and no conditions imposed. The claimant testified that he went to a dentist for his broken teeth but could not recall where or the name of the dentist. He was asked but he also had no letter of attestation or medical report to corroborate when the incident occurred. He further testified that his teeth have been fixed since coming to Canada. The claimant failed to credibly establish that he was being persecuted or that he would be a person of interest to the army or any other group were he to return to Sri Lanka in 2011.

Asked why, if he was allegedly in fear all his life and had been subject to an alleged detention in 2001 and then again in XXXX of 2007, that his sibling (who had been allegedly detained only on one occasion, in XXXX 2006) left in XXXX of 2007 which was before the claimant. The claimant's explanation was that his brother was older and their father did not have enough money to send them both out of the country at the same time. The Tribunal found this explanation insufficient as the Tribunal noted that the claimant testified that his brother had not experienced any problems from XXXX 2006 up to the date of said brother's departure in XXXX of 2007. The Tribunal determined that it did not made sense that a sibling, who had experienced no problems for more than a year, would be sent out of the country when another sibling, namely the claimant, had been detained according to the claimant's narrative before and most recently detained allegedly in XXXX of 2007 and therefore potentially in more imminent danger. The claimant just reiterated that his brother was older so he got to go first.

Further, although asked, it was never clearly or credibly established to the Tribunal who was, is, or would be after the claimant in 2011 and more specifically why. The claimant alluded to a fear of the Sri Lankan army, the LTTE, Tamil militants, and the EPDP who also allegedly abducted his father to extort money in 2006, and yet the claimant never made any efforts to leave Sri Lanka until XXXX of 2008. Asked how many times the claimant was contacted by the LTTE and he indicated that they came to his school once and spoke to all the students in 2001. The LTTE never contacted the claimant again. Notwithstanding that the LTTE were defeated in May of 2009, the Tribunal did not believe that a one time speech at his school constituted persecution by the LTTE. The claimant alleged that his father was abducted by the EPDP on one occasion in XXXX of 2006. Upon payment of 3 Laks, the claimant's father was released. The claimant testified that the EPDP never contacted or threatened his family again. When asked about the alleged army detentions, the claimant admitted that he was never held for more than a day. In light of the ample materials available in the NDP, in addition to the articles submitted on behalf of the claimant3, even if the claimant's allegations regarding the alleged incidents were accepted as fact, the Tribunal did not believe that the treatment as testified to and allegedly experienced by the claimant at the hands of the army amounted to persecution either.

When questioned about what the claimant experienced personally as a young Tamil male in his country, the Tribunal found the claimant's testimony to be vague and lacking in sufficient clarity, detail or corroborative evidence in support. The Tribunal found that the claimant's inability to present any corroborative evidence to credibly establish that he was being sought after, further negatively impacted on his claim.

Asked if there were any conditions upon release on either of the two more recent occasions and he said no. Asked if he suffered any injuries while being detained and he said some. Asked where he went for treatment or for a medical report and he admitted that he had none. Asked why he would be released in such a short period of time with no conditions on each occasion and his response was that he did not know. The Tribunal notes that this was a most volatile period in Sri Lankan history as the LTTE were defeated finally in May of 2009 and up until that point, tensions were such that a Tamil suspected of any connection to the LTTE could be detained indefinitely.4 The claimant did not credibly establish that he had been detained or that he was being persecuted by the military.

The Tribunal is of the view that the National Documentation Package (NDP) is rife with support acknowledging the ill treatment of young Tamil males in Sri Lanka. However, the Tribunal found the testimony of the claimant regarding his alleged detentions by the army not to be credible. The claimant was asked and testified that since his and his brother's respective departures no one has been asking about or looking for the claimant or his brother. By his own testimony, the claimant's father, mother and two sisters continue to reside in Sri Lanka, in the same location, and have not had any problems. Further, the claimant admitted that no one has contacted them regarding his or his brother's whereabouts. The Tribunal does not believe that anyone is or would be looking for the claimant was he to return to Sri Lanka.

Overall, the Tribunal found that the claimant's alleged experiences (if found true) as testified to may have amounted to discrimination and/or harassment, but did not rise to a level of persecution. The Tribunal also noted that by the claimant's own testimony, even if found to be true, he was never held more than a few hours and he had no problems from XXXXXX 2007 through XXXX 2008 when he left Sri Lanka. With regard to the claimant's detention in the U.S. and failing to see his asylum application through, the Tribunal found that the claimant never clearly explained to the Tribunal's satisfaction as to why he was detained for such a lengthy period in the U.S. and further, the Tribunal finds that the claimant's actions in general, were not consistent with those of someone in fear for his life. Asylum Forum Shopping - Delay in claiming

The claimant reached the U.S. and was allegedly detained for a period of one year and seven months. Although asked, the claimant was not initially clear as to whether or not he pursued an asylum claim in the U.S. Many questions had to be asked to obtain clarity regarding his status in the U.S. His PIF question 26 stated that he left before his hearing. During oral testimony he admitted that his claim was rejected in the U.S. It was his appeal allegedly that was pending but he left prior to it being scheduled. Although asked repeatedly, the claimant failed to provide a comprehensive explanation of what occurred in the U.S.

The claimant was allegedly released from custody in the U.S. and then came to Canada on XXXXXX, 2010 and claimed for refugee protection. Asked to produce a copy of his U.S. documents but none were available to be produced into evidence. Asked what the status of his claim was and he said he did not know. Asked what efforts he made to obtain copies of documents and the claimant said that he and his brother tried to contact the U.S. lawyer, six months ago, then three months ago and then two weeks ago but they were not successful. Asked for proof of the attempts to obtain U.S. documentation and the claimant testified that he had nothing. As a result there was nothing to confirm the status of the claimant's asylum matter in the U.S. and nothing to corroborate that the story he presented to the U.S. authorities was the same as before us today.

Asked why, he failed to follow through with his claim in the U.S. but chose to leave there and attempt to enter yet another jurisdiction to file a separate claim in Canada, especially when he was already in the asylum process in the U.S. and the claimant failed to answer. Counsel for the claimant said it was because he had been detained for so long in the U.S. that out of fear he came to Canada. Given the claimant's voluntary abandoning of his U.S. asylum claim by leaving the jurisdiction, the Tribunal found that the claimant's actions were not consistent with those of someone in fear for his life. This also negatively impacted on his credibility. Section 96

While the Tribunal acknowledges that the claimant is a Tamil male, and that Tamils suffer from injustice, discrimination and harassment with, on occasion, as documented in the NDP and the articles submitted on behalf of the claimant5 knowledge of the government, by the claimant's own testimony he failed to credibly establish that he was being persecuted or that he would be in the future. Notwithstanding a nexus, the claimant was not deemed to be a Convention refugee for the reasons set out herein.

Asked whom he feared in his PIF and POE notes, the claimant listed the military, EPDP and LTTE. Incidents with each of the above were addressed in detail in the credibility analysis above. Asked about his detentions and the claimant could provide minimal details. Asked why he would be released so quickly and the claimant could not explain. The Tribunal did not believe that the claimant was seriously being considered a person of interest and that during this volatile period in Sri Lankan history, that the claimant would be released in less than a day on each alleged occasion with no conditions.

The Tribunal found the claimant's account of his alleged detentions and subsequent releases did not identify him as a person of interest in light of what was going on in Sri Lanka at the time. Even if the Tribunal found that the claimant had been detained on the occasions identified, he did not credibly establish that he was being persecuted, nor did the claimant credibly convey to the Tribunal that he would be subject to a serious possibility of being persecuted in the future for any reason, based on the documentary evidence regarding the Government victory over the LTTE in May of 20096 and the recent Danish report7. Given all of the documentation available the Tribunal finds that the claimant failed to meet the criteria for qualifying as a Convention refugee.

The Tribunal notes that, according to the NDP documentation, 2007 was a highly sensitive period in Sri Lanka's history and that the Sri Lankan army was in full force in addressing the long-standing war with the LTTE. The Tribunal also noted that given the breadth of materials in the NDP, the powers of the Sri Lankan government were such that they could hold a suspect indefinitely, and yet, the claimant was supposedly released within a day on each occasion in 2007. As such, the Tribunal found that the claimant was not credible that he was being persecuted based on his race, religion, nationality or membership in a particular social group. Section 97(1)

The Tribunal then considered whether the claimant's removal would subject him personally to the dangers and risks stipulated in Section 97(1). The Federal Court has held that, pursuant to IRPA section 97(1): (i) there must be persuasive evidence (i.e., balance of probabilities) establishing the facts on which a claimant relies. This is to say that the claimant faces a danger or risk of being tortured, risk to life, risk of harm or of having cruel and unusual treatment, or punishment, inflicted upon the claimant's return.8 Section 97(1)(a)

In light of the changes in Sri Lanka9 and the absence of credible evidence to suggest that the army is looking for the claimant or would be were he to return, nothing supported that he would face any danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the "Convention Against Torture", the Tribunal finds that this ground is not open to the claimant. Section 97(1)(b)

The Tribunal then considered whether the claimant is a person who faces a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Notwithstanding the various credibility issues raised, given the change in circumstances in the political environment in Sri Lanka today10, the Tribunal does not believe that it is more likely than not that the claimant would be targeted for any reason were he to return to Sri Lanka. Although the situation in Sri Lanka is not as yet completely resolved, as evidenced by the articles submitted on behalf of the claimant11, the claimant failed to credibly establish to the Tribunal's satisfaction, on a balance of probabilities, that were he to return to Sri Lanka today, he would be of particular interest to the army. The Tribunal did not believe that the claimant is being sought after in his country nor that he would be were he to return to Sri Lanka. Change of Circumstances

Given the claimant's particular circumstances, his profile and the change in circumstances in the political environment in Sri Lanka today12, the Tribunal does not believe that it is more likely than not that the claimant would be targeted were he to return to Sri Lanka. In addition, the Tribunal does not believe that anyone has been looking for the claimant. The Tribunal did not believe that were the claimant to return to Sri Lanka, he would be of any particular interest to the Sri Lankan army or any other militant group.

Further, given the change in circumstances in Sri Lanka today, as established by the documentary evidence, if the claimant had been deemed credible or a Convention refugee, the Tribunal does not believe that it is more likely than not that the claimant would be personally targeted for any reason were he to return to Sri Lanka today. The Tribunal adopts the reasoning of the persuasive decision VA9-0216613, which the Tribunal agrees with, as the claimant in that case was allegedly in somewhat of an analogous situation to the claimant in the present case. Further, the documentary evidence continues to support the fact that there has been a meaningful change of circumstances in Sri Lanka14. Upon raising the issue of a change in circumstances in Sri Lanka in light of the LTTE defeat by the Sri Lankan army in May 200915, which occurred at around the same time as the claimant finally decided to take action and leave Sri Lanka, it could be argued that due to the claimant's Tamil origins, compelling reasons should be considered. Given the change of circumstances in Sri Lanka as documented in the NDP16 and the Danish Immigration Service report17, the Tribunal considered whether the claimant's alleged experiences if ever found to be truthful, constituted atrocious treatment. The Tribunal found that the claimant's case would not merit a finding of compelling reasons. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA)

In the further alternative, the Tribunal concludes that an IFA would be available for the claimant. In order to determine if there is an IFA, the test to be applied is: (i) if there is another part of the country, where the claimant would not have a well-founded fear of persecution and (ii) that it would not be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh to expect the claimant to move to this location.

By the claimant's own testimony, his mother, father and sisters continue to reside in Sri Lanka and have had no problems. During the hearing the claimant was asked if he could relocate to Colombo or Kandy. He did not refute the ability to find a place to live or to obtain work other than to say that though his ID card, they would find him and that because he is a Tamil, no one would give him a job. The claimant provided no documentation to corroborate that anyone is or would be looking for him nor that due to his Tamil ethnicity, he would not be able to find employment in Colombo or Kandy. The claimant testified that he was a XXXX and a XXXX while residing in XXXX. The Tribunal concluded that the claimant did not refute the possibility that he would be able to find employment and a place to live. Further, the NDP documentation18 indicates that restrictions are being eased and registration obligations are only still required in some municipalities. The claimant was asked if he was aware of any warrant for his arrest and he admitted that he was not aware of anything. Having not credibly established to the Tribunal that the authorities or anyone else is looking for the claimant, or that there was a warrant for his arrest pending, and given that the recent documentation pertaining to the situation in Sri Lanka suggests that registration requirements are being eased in a number of locations,19 the Tribunal found that the claimant did not establish that he could not easily relocate to Colombo or Kandy. Given the above factors, the Tribunal did not believe that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh to expect the claimant to move.

Based on the totality of the evidence before it, the Tribunal finds there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted for a section 96 Convention ground if he was to return to Sri Lanka. Nor does the Tribunal find the claimant to be a person in need of protection under section 97 (1)(a) nor section 97(1)(b). As such, he is not a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection.

For all of the reasons cited above, the Tribunal rejects the claim for refugee protection.
